extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulemakers, administrative law scholars, and regulatory policy researchers
extracted.subtask_description: A survey-based evaluation of federal agency rulemakers' perceptions of how electronic rulemaking (e-rulemaking) affects rulemaking tasks, risks, participation quality, and inter-agency coordination. The page enumerates specific activities, worries, and outcome measures that agencies should consider when assessing e-rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct proactive notification and outreach (maintain target mailing lists/listservs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct proactive notification and outreach to the public by maintaining target mailing lists (or listservs) of people who are interested in selected aspects of your rulemaking agendas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey asked whether e-rulemaking made this activity easier or harder; respondents rated this highly positive (average score 5.51), indicating improved ability to do targeted outreach via electronic tools and automated notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and find appropriate stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and find appropriate stakeholders for a given rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured as whether e-rulemaking made stakeholder identification easier; respondents gave moderately positive ratings (avg. 4.81).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disseminate information to generate more informed commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Disseminate information relevant to the agency’s proposed rulemaking (e.g., studies, economic analyses, legal analyses) so as to generate more informed commenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-rulemaking enables posting and linking of related studies and analyses; respondents rated dissemination improvements highly (avg. 5.67).

rubrics_metrics.name: Present competing or multiple alternatives to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Present to the public competing or multiple alternatives to the proposed rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-rulemaking can post alternative drafts and highlight changes; respondents rated this modestly positive (avg. 4.73).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulate public comments generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Stimulate public comments generally (increase participation volume).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Easier public submission (e-mail/online forms) was perceived to increase comment volume (avg. 5.33 for stimulating comments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sort and analyze public comments generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Sort and analyze public comments generally to extract meaningful information for decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents reported e-rulemaking helped with sorting/analysis (avg. 5.02), but concerns about volume and manipulability remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain public comments targeted to particular portions/segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain public comments specifically addressed to particular portions or segments of the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segmenting proposed rules and using forms/threads can target comments; perceived benefit was only mildly positive (avg. 4.64).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sort and analyze comments for specific portions/segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Sort and analyze public comments specifically addressed to particular portions or segments of the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents reported only modest gains in this ability (avg. 4.70), indicating a need for better tools or processes for targeted analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reply comments (allow replies to others' comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enable the concept of 'reply comments' so commenters can respond to what others have said (not new issues but direct replies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-rulemaking can allow threaded replies; respondents saw this positively (avg. 5.44) and noted it could help agencies address comments more efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place summaries of ex parte communications in the record more quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Place summaries of ex parte communications in the record more quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic publication can accelerate posting of ex parte summaries; respondents reported improvement (avg. 5.16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate rulemaking internally (multiple staff access to the same docket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate the rulemaking internally by allowing many people to look at the same rulemaking docket without getting in each other's way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic dockets enable simultaneous access and internal coordination; respondents rated this highest among activities (avg. 5.70).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate rulemaking externally with OMB/other government entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate the rulemaking externally with OMB or other interested government entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-rulemaking facilitates interagency sharing; respondents perceived improvement (avg. 5.23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct interactive proceedings (e.g., negotiated rulemaking, deliberative dialogues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct interactive proceedings in rulemaking, such as 'negotiated rulemaking' or online deliberative dialogues/chatrooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite proposals for interactive formats, respondents were mixed and gave low-to-moderate scores (avg. 4.19), suggesting limited realized benefit so far.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft a final-rule preamble that responds to comments and includes relevant analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft a preamble to the final rule that responds to comments and includes all relevant studies and analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-rulemaking can aggregate materials to inform preambles; respondents saw a positive effect (avg. 5.05).

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and implement appropriate archival practices for rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop and implement appropriate archival practices relating to rulemakings (such as retiring records, scanning/retention practices, long-term access).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic records create new archival needs; respondents saw improvements but also noted challenges (avg. 5.25).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodically evaluate and review promulgated rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodically evaluate and review the rule (and related rules) once promulgated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-rulemaking supports ongoing review and monitoring of rules; respondents reported positive effects (avg. 5.19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational goal: provide global, seamless access and vertical drill-down of rulemaking materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide access to every meaningful step in the generation of a rule (from authorizing statute through final rule, court challenges, amendments, interpretations, enforcement actions) and enable 'drilling down' into related studies/analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an articulated success criterion for transformative e-rulemaking: comprehensive, linked, searchable dockets that present a vertical and horizontal view of rulemaking history and related materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participatory goal: enable real-time, interactive stakeholder participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Enable participants to participate in real time with other stakeholders in a rulemaking process (e.g., chat rooms, threaded discussions) to promote more rational, interactive, and less adversarial rule development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success measured by whether e-tools support deliberative dialogue, targeted contribution, and interactive exchange rather than simple mass submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outside intervention risk (hacking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk of outside intervention ('hacking') into rulemaking proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey measured increased worry about hacking; agency concern is whether e-systems are secure against unauthorized manipulation or intrusion (avg. 3.32 — more worried).

rubrics_metrics.name: Virus risk from attachments submitted in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk of acquiring viruses via attachments submitted in comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic attachments raise malware risk to agency systems; respondents expressed increased worry (avg. 3.31).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate exposure of confidential business information
rubrics_metrics.description: Inappropriate exposure of materials in the rulemaking docket that might contain confidential business information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making dockets public online increases risk that CBI will be exposed; respondents were notably worried (avg. 3.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate exposure of copyrighted materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Inappropriate exposure of materials in the rulemaking docket that might contain copyrighted materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posting documents online risks copyright infringement or disputed exposure; respondents expressed concern (avg. 3.20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate exposure of indecent or obscene materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Inappropriate exposure of materials in the rulemaking docket that might contain indecent or obscene language or materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public posting could expose readers to offensive content; respondents worried to an extent (avg. 3.30).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate exposure raising national security concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Inappropriate exposure of information in the rulemaking docket that might lead to national security problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some docket materials may implicate security; respondents were less worried overall but this remains a concern (avg. 3.82).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of information-destruction or irretrievable loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk of information-destruction or other irretrievable loss of rulemaking information in electronic systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns about digital preservation and backups exist; respondents rated this slightly less worrying than other risks (avg. 4.09 = somewhat less worried than 'more worried').

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrating scanned paper comments with electronically submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to integrate (scanned) paper comments with e-mailed or electronically submitted comments into a coherent docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents found e-rulemaking has eased integration somewhat (avg. 4.14) but technical/process issues remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of comments (ensuring submissions are genuine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authenticity of comments — ensuring that comments are submitted by the persons they claim to be and are not fraudulent or automated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns about bots, form letters, and duplicate submissions make authenticity a key criterion (avg. 3.81 indicated increased worry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of commenters' privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensuring the protection of the privacy of commenters when comments and contact information are published online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online publication makes personal data exposure more likely; respondents were worried (avg. 3.13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number (volume) of comments received
rubrics_metrics.description: Change in the number of public comments received with advent of e-rulemaking (volume increase or decrease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey measured whether agencies received more comments; most reported increases (avg. 5.36 = more comments). Volume is an outcome metric and affects processing burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of comments that provide new useful information or arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether comments provide new, useful information or arguments that inform agency decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents were split and on average saw little change (avg. 3.8 ≈ same); this is a quality metric distinct from volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of comments that are opinions without supporting facts/arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Amount of comments that provide only opinions without supporting facts or arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-rulemaking was perceived to increase such comments (many respondents reported more opinion-only submissions); this indicates potential decline in comment substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of identical or near-identical comments (form comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevalence of comments that are identical or nearly identical (form letters, mass submissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant increases reported (many respondents observed many more identical comments), raising concerns about deliberative value and processing burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value placed on comments of the average citizen
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether agencies place more, less, or the same value on comments submitted by average citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three-fourths reported no change in value placed on average citizen comments (avg. 4.27), making this an evaluative normative measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of commenters responding to others' comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether more commenters are responding to comments already in the docket (i.e., meta-discussion among commenters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some respondents noted increases, suggesting potential for interactive deliberation (20 yes vs 16 no in one question).

rubrics_metrics.name: References to economic analyses and supporting documents by commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether commenters make more references to economic analyses and other supporting documents in the docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents largely did not observe a large increase (7 yes, 22 no, many don't know), so this quality improvement is not strongly evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of questions received by agency offices about ongoing rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Change in the number of questions to agency offices about ongoing rulemakings (public inquiries seeking clarification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slight increase reported (avg. 4.21), indicating more engagement or confusion requiring agency response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to consult with and learn from counterparts in other agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: How much opportunity agency rulemakers had to consult with and learn from counterparts in other agencies about e-rulemaking issues, and adequacy of that opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most reported some opportunity but many found it less than adequate; interagency learning and shared best practices are an evaluative concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for politicization/referendum-like weighting of comments (volume over substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk that mass electronic commenting will lead agencies or courts to treat comment tallies as referendum-like evidence of public preference, rather than as substantive input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly critiques warn that agencies may resort to crude 'for/against' tallies when faced with huge volumes, which would undermine the technocratic/substantive nature of rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of information-filtering and near-duplicate detection tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to use information-filtering technologies (e.g., near-duplicate detection) to sort, cluster, and identify duplicate or near-duplicate comments efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical solutions are being developed (cited research) and are an important criterion for whether agencies can manage e-rulemaking information overload effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/procedural sufficiency of electronic notice (Federal Register vs. internet-only notice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether electronic notices satisfy the APA notice requirement (internet-only notice may not suffice; Federal Register publication remains legally required in many contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Util. Solid Waste Activities Group v. EPA) indicates the APA's notice requirement is not met by internet-only notice; legal sufficiency of notice is a core procedural criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of attachments, authentication, security, privacy, and copyright issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Address technical and legal issues including handling of attachments, authentication of submitters, system security, protection of privacy, and copyright concerns in electronic dockets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are enumerated technical/legal challenges that must be resolved for e-rulemaking to be transformative; they are both success criteria and constraints on system design.
